newsitem.title: USA: Attorney says police set to end Texas standoff.
newsitem.headline: Attorney says police set to end Texas standoff.

text.p: An attorney for a Texas separatist group said on Friday that police were in "full battle gear" and ready to move in to end a six-day standoff in the mountains of west Texas.

Attorney Terence O'Rourke told reporters he feared a bloodbath was imminent and pleaded with Texas Gov. George W. Bush to order the dozens of troopers ringing the rebel compound to stand down to give him more time to negotiate a peaceful solution to the standoff.
O'Rourke said he had been told indirectly that Bush had agreed to intervene, but Bush spokeswoman Karen Hughes told Reuters: "That is absolutely false."
She said the governor was leaving all decisions up to the Texas Department of Public Safety (DPS).
O'Rourke, who spoke as he left the police command centre near the Republic of Texas compound, said elite police squads brought in to confront the rebels looked battle-ready.
"They are in position to go in and execute the arrest warrants, and I am convinced that will mean the death of some or all of the people inside," O'Rourke said.
"I am pleading with Gov. Bush for mercy, to give us a little more time, just a little more time," he said.
The siege began on Sunday when members of the Republic, which claims that Texas is an independent nation, took two hostages in retaliation for the arrest of their security chief, Robert Scheidt.

The hostages were later released in exchange for Scheidt, but felony charges were filed against six of the Republic members. Scheidt became the first of the rebels to give up when he walked out of the compound on Friday and surrendered without incident.
Police said Scheidt told them he was "desperate" to get out.

O'Rourke said there appeared to be divisions developing among the 12 rebels left in the tin-walled compound, but that McLaren and others were ready to die for their cause. He said he had received letters from eight of those inside telling their families goodbye because they expected to be killed.
Also, O'Rourke said McLaren sent out a note firing him as his attorney, but he would not accept it until he had spoken with McLaren face-to-face, which police have not permitted.

The day's events darkened what had been a mood of growing optimism after Scheidt left the group. Police, who did not comment about O'Rourke's fear that invasion was imminent, said Scheidt's surrender was a hopeful sign they could negotiate an end to the standoff.
"We are encouraged that none of our contingency planning is going to have to come into effect, at least in the immediate term," DPS spokesman Mike Cox said.

Police have surrounded the complex and brought in helicopters, two police armoured personnel carriers and bloodhounds. They have pledged to execute the arrest warrants if they cannot negotiate a peaceful end to the standoff, but also say they want a peaceful end.

Officials said they were concerned the siege was becoming a rallying point for anti-government militias after arresting at least nine armed men in the area this week on their way to fight alongside the separatists.

The Republic of Texas group, formed in 1995, believes the 1845 annexation of Texas by the United States was illegal. Texas was an independent nation for nine years after breaking away from Mexico in 1836.
